thread.title: What S.4009 Could Change for Forced Organ Harvesting Accountability
thread.title_full: What S.4009 Could Change for Forced Organ Harvesting Accountability

author: Yin Hua
title: What S.4009 Could Change for Forced Organ Harvesting Accountability
text:
WASHINGTON D.C. — The U.S. Senate’s passage of legislation targeting forced organ harvesting in China represents more than another congressional condemnation of human rights abuses.
If enacted, the Falun Gong and Victims of Forced Organ Harvesting Protection Act (S.4009), which was passed unanimously on Sept. 28, would give the executive branch concrete obligations, including investigating China’s transplant system, identifying foreign individuals implicated in forced organ harvesting, and imposing financial and immigration sanctions against those involved.
That distinguishes the measure from earlier congressional resolutions, which expressed concern and called for action but did not themselves create binding sanctions requirements. Because the Senate-approved text differs from legislation previously passed by the House, further House action is required before the measure can reach the president’s desk to be signed into law.
RELATED: US Senate Passes Bipartisan Bill Targeting Forced Organ Harvesting in China
From resolutions to sanctions
Congress has addressed forced organ harvesting allegations in China before. In 2016, the House unanimously passed H.Res.343, which condemned what it described as persistent reports of state-sanctioned forced organ harvesting from prisoners of conscience and other marginalized groups, including Falun Gong practitioners. The resolution called on Beijing to end the practice, urged an independent investigation and asked the State Department to provide more detailed reporting.

Falun Gong, also known as Falun Dafa, is a spiritual practice rooted in the principles of Truthfulness, Compassion, and Forbearance. Despite being peaceful in nature, the CCP launched a brutal campaign to eradicate the practice in July 1999 after seeing its rapid rise in popularity as a threat to its authoritarian regime. Since then, thousands of practitioners have perished at the hands of Chinese police, with many today still undergoing routine monitoring, arbitrary travel bans, and arrests.
However, analysts note that a House resolution is fundamentally different from legislation enacted into federal law. S.4009 would require the president to impose sanctions on foreign persons determined to have knowingly and directly engaged in or facilitated forced organ harvesting within China. The Senate bill defines forced organ harvesting broadly, including organ removal obtained through coercion, abduction, deception, fraud, abuse of power or exploitation of vulnerability.
Those measures could include blocking property under U.S. jurisdiction and barring designated individuals from entering the United States. That shift, from urging action to requiring specified action, is the central significance supporters see in the legislation.
Increased accountability
The bill would also move responsibility for investigating the allegations more firmly into the U.S. government. Under the Senate text, the secretary of state, in consultation with the Department of Health and Human Services, National Institutes of Health and relevant intelligence agencies, would be required to produce a detailed assessment of China’s organ transplantation system.
The report would examine the number of transplants performed annually, the estimated number of voluntary donors, organ sources, waiting times and evidence concerning systemic forced organ harvesting. It would also require the U.S. government to determine whether Beijing currently engages, or previously engaged, in systematic forced organ harvesting and, if so, assess whether the conduct constitutes an atrocity under U.S. law.
China analyst Heng He argued that government involvement could significantly change the investigative landscape. Previously, he said, much of the work documenting alleged abuses depended on nongovernmental investigators who faced substantial obstacles gathering evidence inside China. A formal federal inquiry, he argued, would give investigators access to resources and government-to-government channels unavailable to private groups.
Building on House legislation
The Senate measure also draws on legislation already approved by the House. In May 2025, lawmakers passed the Falun Gong Protection Act (H.R.1540), which establishes a U.S. policy of seeking to end state-sponsored forced organ harvesting in China and requires sanctions against foreign persons knowingly involved in the practice. The bill specifically calls for asset freezes and visa restrictions.
The House also advanced the Stop Forced Organ Harvesting Act of 2025 (H.R.1503), a broader measure addressing organ trafficking and forced harvesting beyond China alone. S.4009 incorporates elements of those approaches while maintaining a specific focus on forced organ harvesting within China and prisoners of conscience, including Falun Gong practitioners.
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), who introduced the Senate bill with Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.), said following its passage that the measure was intended to translate congressional concern into accountability. “The Chinese Communist Party continues to target Falun Gong practitioners through its brutal, state-sponsored organ harvesting industry. These atrocities are an assault on religious liberty and fundamental human rights,” Cruz said in a Sept. 29 statement.
He added, “I am proud to have worked with Senator Merkley to get this bipartisan bill through the Senate, and I urge my colleagues in the House to pass it and send it to the President’s desk.”
What the bill would do
The measure would not itself prove individual allegations of organ harvesting, nor would Senate passage immediately freeze anyone’s assets or bar them from entering the United States. Those consequences depend first on the bill becoming law and then on federal authorities identifying individuals who meet the statutory requirements for designation.
That distinction is important. The legislation would create a framework for investigation and punishment rather than pre-determine who is responsible.
It would also increase transparency around U.S. involvement in transplant research. The State Department report would be required to identify federal grants awarded during the previous decade that supported organ-transplant research in China or collaboration between American and Chinese institutions.
The House is now the key hurdle
For S.4009 to become law, the House and Senate ultimately must approve identical legislative text. The House has already demonstrated bipartisan support for related legislation, but the Senate’s amended measure must still clear the remaining legislative process before reaching the White House. Until that happens, S.4009 remains proposed legislation rather than an enforceable sanctions regime.
Still, the distinction from earlier congressional action is clear, meaning where previous resolutions primarily documented concerns and urged government action, the Senate bill would, if enacted, require federal agencies to investigate the allegations and provide a mechanism to impose consequences on individuals found responsible.
For advocates who have spent years pressing governments to investigate allegations of forced organ harvesting in China, that transition, from condemnation to potential enforcement, is what makes S.4009 materially different.

S.4009 incorporates elements of those approaches while maintaining a specific focus on forced organ harvesting within China and prisoners of conscience, including Falun Gong practitioners.
